<reason>Both sides were disciplined, format-compliant, and free of fake precision. A opened with a clean principle (barriers should track burden) and landed real hits: the identity-vs-competence distinction, the revocability inversion (years-long removal vs one-click delisting), and honest A1/A2 answers naming accountancy and software as a non-trivial middle. But B controlled the decisive ground. B accepted A's principle, redefined the relevant burden as cost-of-error to relying parties, and then converted A's licensing concession into a structural fork: the motion is either empty (remote low-risk work already runs without state recognition) or dangerous (where the stamp matters, A concedes full local licensing). A's middle-ground escape — financial, discoverable, insurable harms — was effectively rebranded by B as "a cleanup crew, not a gate," and A never resolved the dilemma that the stamp either replaces firm scrutiny (manufactured reliance on competence the state cannot verify) or is decorative. B's closing sharpened this into one memorable line; A's closing mostly restated. B answered A's pressure questions by folding them into the fork, while A's answers, though responsive, fed B's frame. B wins on rebuttal decisiveness, framing, and rhetorical force.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 fork: A's concession that high-risk professions "would still require local licensing" meant the fast lane survives only where stakes are trivial — "the carve-out IS the debate" — later completed in Rebuttal 2 as "the motion is either empty or dangerous," plus the lethal "revocation without detection is a receipt, not a remedy" answer to A's one-click delisting point.</best_rebuttal>
